\chapter{Introducing Yourself}
\label{ch:introductions}
\hlchaptermodality{2}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can give my name and ask for someone else's in Hindi, and write \hi{मेरा} \hi{नाम} and \hi{नमस्ते} by hand.}

Assemble \hi{नमस्ते} from \hi{न}, \hi{म}, \hi{स्} and \hi{ते} under a single head-line, then say the bow the word literally names.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\hi{नाम}]{\hi{नाम} (nām) — \textquotedblleft{}name,\textquotedblright{} a word older than Europe}

\label{lesson:HI-C02-naam}



\begin{quote}
To introduce yourself you need \textquotedblleft{}name.\textquotedblright{} Hindi's is one you already own in English — from before either language was born.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Devanagari.)} Left to right: \textbf{\hi{न}} (na) + \textbf{\hi{ा}} (the long-\emph{ā} mātrā) $\to$ \textbf{\hi{ना}} (nā), then \textbf{\hi{म}} (ma). Read \textbf{\hi{ना}·\hi{म}} $\to$ \textbf{nām}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\hi{नाम}} (\emph{nām}) $\leftarrow$ Sanskrit \textbf{\hi{नामन्}} (\emph{nāman}), from Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*h\textsubscript{3}nómn} (its final \emph{n} syllabic) — the \emph{same} ancient root as:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item English \textbf{name}, Latin \textbf{nōmen} ($\to$ English \textbf{noun}, \textbf{nom}inate), Greek \emph{onoma}.
\end{itemize}

So Hindi \emph{nām} and English \emph{name} are cousins from before either language existed — one of the clearest bridges between the Indian and European branches of one family.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{sounds}
Three letters, left to right: \hi{न} (\emph{na}), \hi{ा} the long-ā \emph{mātrā} (\hi{ना} = nā), \hi{म} (\emph{ma}). Read \hi{ना}·\hi{म} $\to$ \emph{nām}.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nām\textquotedblright{}
  \item the cousins — Hindi \emph{nām}, English \emph{name}, Latin \emph{nōmen} $\to$ \emph{noun}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Sanskrit and PIE root is \textbf{\hi{नाम}} from, and what English words share it? (\emph{nāman} / \emph{*h\textsubscript{3}nómn} — \emph{name}, \emph{noun}, \emph{nominate}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[merā]{\hi{मेरा} (merā) — \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:HI-C02-meraa}



\begin{quote}
The word for \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{} — and, like \emph{name}, a first-person word English shares to the root.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Devanagari.)} \textbf{\hi{म}} (ma) + \textbf{\hi{े}} (the \emph{e}-mātrā) $\to$ \textbf{\hi{मे}} (me); \textbf{\hi{र}} (ra) + \textbf{\hi{ा}} (long \emph{ā}) $\to$ \textbf{\hi{रा}} (rā). Read \textbf{\hi{मे}·\hi{रा}} $\to$ \textbf{merā}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\hi{मेरा}} (\emph{merā}, \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{}) descends from Sanskrit \emph{madīya} (\textquotedblleft{}of me\textquotedblright{}), on the first-person root \textbf{ma-} — the \emph{same} \emph{ma-/me-} behind English \textbf{me}, \textbf{my}, \textbf{mine} and Latin \emph{meus}. Hindi \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{} and English \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{} are, at root, one word.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{} agrees with the noun}]
Hindi possessives change to match what's owned: \textbf{merā} (masculine), \textbf{merī} (feminine), \textbf{mere} (plural). \emph{nām} is masculine $\to$ \textbf{merā nām}. (You'll meet \emph{merī} at your first feminine noun.)
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{sounds}
\hi{म} (\emph{ma}) + \hi{े} (the \emph{e}-mātrā) $\to$ \hi{मे} (me); then \hi{र} (\emph{ra}) + \hi{ा} (long ā) $\to$ \hi{रा} (rā). Read \hi{मे}·\hi{रा} $\to$ \emph{merā}.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}merā\textquotedblright{}
  \item the cousins — \emph{merā} / English \emph{my}, \emph{mine}
  \item the three forms — merā (m.) / merī (f.) / mere (pl.)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What root is \textbf{\hi{मेरा}} built on, and its English cousins? (\emph{ma-} — \emph{me}, \emph{my}, \emph{mine}.) Why \emph{merā nām} and not \emph{merī}? (\emph{nām} is masculine.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hai]{\hi{है} (hai) — \textquotedblleft{}is,\textquotedblright{} cousin of English \emph{is}}

\label{lesson:HI-C02-hai}



\begin{quote}
The little verb \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{} — and it's the same \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{} spoken from Ireland to India.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Devanagari.)} \textbf{\hi{ह}} (ha) + \textbf{\hi{ै}} (the \emph{ai}-mātrā) $\to$ \textbf{\hi{है}} (\emph{hai}). One syllable.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\hi{है}} (\emph{hai}, \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Sanskrit \textbf{\hi{अस्ति}} (\emph{asti}, \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{}), from Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*h\textsubscript{1}es-} — the root of \textquotedblleft{}to be\textquotedblright{} across the whole family:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item English \textbf{is}, German \textbf{ist}, Latin \textbf{est}, Spanish \textbf{es}, French \textbf{est}.
\end{itemize}

Hindi \emph{hai} is the Indian cousin of the same tiny verb. \textquotedblleft{}Is\textquotedblright{} really is \emph{one} word, stretched across a continent.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the verb comes last}]
Hindi is \textbf{subject–object–verb}: \textquotedblleft{}my name Arun \textbf{is}.\textquotedblright{} \emph{hai} sits at the \emph{end} of the sentence, where English puts \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{} in the middle. Bank the shape — in Hindi the verb waits until the end.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{sounds}
\hi{ह} (\emph{ha}) + \hi{ै} (the \emph{ai}-mātrā) $\to$ \hi{है} (\emph{hai}). One syllable.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hai\textquotedblright{}
  \item the family — \emph{hai} / \emph{is} / \emph{ist} / \emph{est} / \emph{es}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}merā nām Arun hai\textquotedblright{} — note \emph{hai} at the end
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Sanskrit/PIE root is \textbf{\hi{है}} from, and its cousins? (\emph{asti} / \emph{*h\textsubscript{1}es-} — \emph{is}, \emph{ist}, \emph{est}, \emph{es}.) Where does the verb sit in a Hindi sentence? (At the end.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\hi{मेरा} \hi{नाम} … \hi{है}]{\hi{मेरा} \hi{नाम} … \hi{है} (merā nām … hai) — \textquotedblleft{}my name is…\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:HI-C02-mera-naam-hai}



\begin{quote}
Assemble the three atoms you just traced — \emph{merā}, \emph{nām}, \emph{hai} — into the sentence for meeting anyone.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The two words — assembled}
Three atoms, each already rooted — merā (my, $\leftarrow$ \emph{ma-}), nām (name, $\leftarrow$ \emph{nāman}), hai (is, $\leftarrow$ \emph{asti}):

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{मेरा} \hi{नाम} … \hi{है}} = \textquotedblleft{}my name … is\textquotedblright{} = \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}my name is…\textquotedblright{}}
\end{quote}

\emph{Merā nām Arun hai.} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}My name is Arun.\textquotedblright{} Slot your name into the gap; \emph{hai} stays at the end.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: subject–object–verb}]
Literally the Hindi is \textquotedblleft{}my name Arun \textbf{is}\textquotedblright{} — the verb last. English puts \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{} in the middle (\textquotedblleft{}my name \textbf{is} Arun\textquotedblright{}); Hindi holds it to the end. Every Hindi sentence you build will end on its verb.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}merā nām … hai\textquotedblright{} with your own name
  \item notice the order — my / name / {[}name{]} / is
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give your name in Hindi. (\emph{Merā nām … hai.}) What's different about where \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{} sits, versus English? (Hindi puts the verb \emph{last}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\hi{आप} / \hi{तुम}]{\hi{आप} / \hi{तुम} (āp / tum) — \textquotedblleft{}you,\textquotedblright{} respectful and familiar}

\label{lesson:HI-C02-aap-tum}



\begin{quote}
To ask someone's name, you need \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} — and Hindi grades it in \emph{three} levels of respect.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Devanagari.)} \textbf{\hi{आप}}: independent vowel \textbf{\hi{आ}} (ā, word-initial) + \textbf{\hi{प}} (pa) $\to$ \emph{āp}. \textbf{\hi{तुम}}: \textbf{\hi{त}} (ta) + \textbf{\hi{ु}} (the \emph{u}-sign) + \textbf{\hi{म}} (ma) $\to$ \emph{tum}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{तुम}} (\emph{tum}, familiar \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Sanskrit \emph{tvam}, from PIE \textbf{*tū} — the same root as English archaic \textbf{thou}, Latin \emph{tū}, French \emph{tu}.
  \item \textbf{\hi{आप}} (\emph{āp}, respectful \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{}) is a separate honorific word (originally \textquotedblleft{}oneself\textquotedblright{}).
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: three levels of \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{}}]
Hindi grades respect three ways: \textbf{āp} (respectful — strangers, elders), \textbf{tum} (familiar — friends, peers), \textbf{tū} (intimate or to a child; can insult if misused). The European tracks had two levels each; Hindi has three. For a first meeting, always \textbf{āp}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{sounds}
\hi{आप}: the independent vowel \hi{आ} (ā, word-initial) + \hi{प} (\emph{pa}) $\to$ \emph{āp}. \hi{तुम}: \hi{त} (\emph{ta}) + \hi{ु} (the \emph{u}-sign) + \hi{म} (\emph{ma}) $\to$ \emph{tum}.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}āp\textquotedblright{} (respectful), \textquotedblleft{}tum\textquotedblright{} (familiar)
  \item the cousin of \emph{tum} — archaic English \emph{thou}
  \item which to use with a stranger (\emph{āp})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Name Hindi's three \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{}s and when \emph{āp} is used. (\emph{āp} / \emph{tum} / \emph{tū}; \emph{āp} for respect, strangers, first meetings.) What English word is \emph{tum}'s cousin? (\emph{thou}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kyā]{\hi{क्या} (kyā) — \textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:HI-C02-kya}



\begin{quote}
German asks a name with \textquotedblleft{}how\textquotedblright{}; Hindi uses \textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{} — so here's \emph{kyā}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(Skim if you read Devanagari.)} A \textbf{conjunct}: \textbf{\hi{क}} (ka) loses its vowel (a \emph{halant}) and joins \textbf{\hi{य}} (ya) $\to$ \textbf{\hi{क्य}} (kya); add the long-\emph{ā} mātrā $\to$ \textbf{\hi{क्या}} (\emph{kyā}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\hi{क्या}} (\emph{kyā}, \textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Sanskrit \emph{kim} / the interrogative stem \textbf{ka-}, from PIE \textbf{*k\textsuperscript{w}o-} — the same question-root behind English \textbf{wh-} words (\textbf{what}, \textbf{who}, \textbf{which}) and Latin \textbf{qu-}. Hindi's question-words nearly all start with this \textbf{k-}: \emph{kyā} (what), \emph{kaun} (who), \emph{kab} (when), \emph{kyūn} (why).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{sounds}
A \textbf{conjunct}: \hi{क} (\emph{ka}) loses its vowel (\emph{halant}) and joins \hi{य} (\emph{ya}) $\to$ \hi{क्य} (\emph{kya}); add the long-ā mātrā $\to$ \hi{क्या} (\emph{kyā}).
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kyā\textquotedblright{}
  \item the English \emph{wh-} cousins — what, who, which
  \item the Hindi \emph{k-} question family — kyā, kaun, kab
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What root is \textbf{\hi{क्या}} from, and its English cousins? (\emph{ka-} / \emph{*k\textsuperscript{w}o-} — \emph{what}, \emph{who}, \emph{which}.) What sound do most Hindi question-words start with? (\emph{k-}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\hi{आपका} \hi{नाम} \hi{क्या} \hi{है}?]{\hi{आपका} \hi{नाम} \hi{क्या} \hi{है}? (āpkā nām kyā hai?) — \textquotedblleft{}what's your name?\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:HI-C02-aapka-naam-kya-hai}



\begin{quote}
Assemble the question: your + name + what + is.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The two words — assembled}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{आपका}} (\emph{āpkā}, \textquotedblleft{}your\textquotedblright{}) = \textbf{\hi{आप}} (you) + \textbf{\hi{का}} (\emph{kā}, the possessive \textquotedblleft{}of,\textquotedblright{} the same agreeing \emph{kā/kī/ke} that matches the noun).
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{आपका} \hi{नाम} \hi{क्या} \hi{है}?} = literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{your name what is?}\textquotedblright{} = \textquotedblleft{}what's your name?\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Hindi keeps the verb \textbf{last} again, and simply drops the question-word \emph{kyā} into the object slot — no reordering, no inversion.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: answer, and the informal version}]
Answer with the sentence you built: \textbf{Merā nām Arun hai.} The informal \textquotedblleft{}your\textquotedblright{} swaps \emph{āpkā} for \textbf{tumhārā}: \emph{tumhārā nām kyā hai?}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}āpkā nām kyā hai?\textquotedblright{}
  \item ask, then answer — \textquotedblleft{}āpkā nām kyā hai?\textquotedblright{} / \textquotedblleft{}merā nām … hai\textquotedblright{}
  \item the informal — \textquotedblleft{}tumhārā nām kyā hai?\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\hi{आपका} \hi{नाम} \hi{क्या} \hi{है}?} literally say, and where's the verb? (\textquotedblleft{}Your name what is?\textquotedblright{}; the verb \emph{hai} is last.) What's \emph{āpkā} made of? (\emph{āp} + \emph{kā}, \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} + possessive.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\hi{ख़ुशी}]{\hi{ख़ुशी} (khushī) — \textquotedblleft{}happiness,\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}pleased to meet you\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:HI-C02-khushi}



\begin{quote}
The close to an introduction — and a word from Hindi's \emph{other} vocabulary.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The two words}
The Hindi \textquotedblleft{}pleased to meet you\textquotedblright{} is \textbf{\hi{आपसे} \hi{मिलकर} \hi{ख़ुशी} \hi{हुई}} (\emph{āp-se milkar khushī huī}) — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{having met you, happiness happened}.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{cousinweb}
The key word \textbf{\hi{ख़ुशी}} (\emph{khushī}, \textquotedblleft{}happiness\textquotedblright{}) is \textbf{not} Sanskrit — it's \textbf{Persian} (\emph{khush}, \textquotedblleft{}happy, pleasant\textquotedblright{}), one of the thousands of Persian words in everyday Hindi. (The dot under \textbf{\hi{ख़}} — a \emph{nukta} — marks the Persian \emph{kh} sound.) So even introducing yourself draws on Hindi's \textbf{two} vocabularies: Sanskrit (\emph{nām}, \emph{hai}) and Perso-Arabic (\emph{khushī}) — the same double heritage you met with \emph{shukriyā} and \emph{alvidā} in Chapter 1.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}āpse milkar khushī huī\textquotedblright{}
  \item the key word — \emph{khushī} (\textquotedblleft{}happiness\textquotedblright{}), a Persian word
  \item the two heritages — Sanskrit \emph{nām}, Persian \emph{khushī}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the Hindi \textquotedblleft{}pleased to meet you\textquotedblright{} literally mean, and where is \emph{khushī} from? (\textquotedblleft{}Having met you, happiness happened\textquotedblright{}; Persian.) What does the \emph{nukta} dot under \hi{ख़} mark? (A Persian/Arabic sound.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ā, e]{Mātrās — swapping the built-in vowel}

\label{lesson:HI-W03-matras-naam}



\begin{quote}
Last lesson: every consonant carries a free \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}a\textquotedblright{}}. So how do you write \emph{ni}, or \emph{mo}, or \emph{nā}?

You \textbf{overwrite} the inherent vowel with a small mark called a \textbf{mātrā}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The word itself}
\textbf{\hi{मात्रा}} (\emph{mātrā}) means \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}a measure\textquotedblright{}} — from the verb \emph{mā-}, \textquotedblleft{}to measure.\textquotedblright{} That root is Proto-Indo-European *\emph{meh\textsubscript{1}-}, and it is the ancestor of English \textbf{meter}, \textbf{measure}, \textbf{immense} (\textquotedblleft{}un-measurable\textquotedblright{}), and — by the oldest measuring instrument of all — \textbf{month}, the moon being what humans first counted time with.

A vowel sign is a \emph{measure} of the syllable. The name is a description.

\subsection*{You'll want to know — Two to start with}
\textbf{\hi{ा}} — the vowel \textbf{ā} (a long \textquotedblleft{}aa\textquotedblright{}). A vertical bar to the \textbf{right}:

\begin{quote}
\hi{न} + \hi{ा} $\to$ \textbf{\hi{ना}} (\emph{nā})
\end{quote}

\textbf{\hi{े}} — the vowel \textbf{e}. A stroke \textbf{above} the top bar:

\begin{quote}
\hi{म} + \hi{े} $\to$ \textbf{\hi{मे}} (\emph{me})
\end{quote}

Notice the mātrā did not \emph{add} a vowel. It \textbf{replaced} one. \hi{न} was already \textquotedblleft{}na\textquotedblright{}; now it is \textquotedblleft{}nā\textquotedblright{}. The inherent vowel is gone the moment a mātrā arrives.

\subsection*{You'll want to know — Now write a word you already know}
You have \hi{न}, \hi{ा}, \hi{म}. That is enough for the Hindi word for \textquotedblleft{}name\textquotedblright{} (Chapter 2):

\begin{quote}
\hi{न} + \hi{ा} + \hi{म} $\to$ \textbf{\hi{नाम}} (\emph{nām})
\end{quote}

Write the three characters, then draw \textbf{one bar} across all of them.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \hi{ना} — \textquotedblleft{}na, then the bar to the right\textquotedblright{} — \emph{nā}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \hi{मे} — \textquotedblleft{}ma, then the stroke above\textquotedblright{} — \emph{me}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \textbf{\hi{नाम}} — three characters, \textbf{one bar}, \textquotedblleft{}nām\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{\hi{मात्रा}} = a \textbf{measure}\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does a mātrā do to the inherent vowel? (\textbf{Replaces} it — never adds to it.) What does the word \emph{mātrā} mean, and what English words share its root? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{Measure}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{meter}, \emph{measure}, \emph{month}.) Where does \textbf{\hi{ा}} attach, and where does \textbf{\hi{े}}? (Right; above the bar.) Write \textbf{\hi{नाम}} — what does it mean? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{Name}\textquotedblright{}.) Next: the one mātrā whose position tries to fool your eye.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[i]{\hi{ि} — left on the page, right in the mouth}

\label{lesson:HI-W03-preposed-i}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{ा}} sits to the right and \textbf{\hi{े}} above. One Hindi vowel sign goes somewhere that will feel wrong for a while.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The famous mātrā}
\textbf{\hi{ि}} — the vowel \textbf{i} — is written \textbf{before} the consonant, to its \textbf{left}, but pronounced \textbf{after} it:

\begin{quote}
\hi{श} + \hi{ि} $\to$ \textbf{\hi{शि}}, and that says \emph{\textbf{śi}}, not \emph{iś}.
\end{quote}

Read it aloud in the order you might guess and you get the wrong word. The mark \emph{leans left} on the page and \emph{lands right} in the mouth.

There is no satisfying modern logic behind the placement. It comes down from the script's Brahmi ancestry and simply stuck. Your eye will learn it faster than your intuition will.

The rule to carry away:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{A mātrā replaces the inherent vowel. And \hi{ि} — the only Hindi mātrā that does this — is written before the consonant it follows.}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \hi{ि} + \hi{श} as the visual order in \textbf{\hi{शि}}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}śi — the mark leans left and lands right\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \textbf{\hi{ना}} \emph{nā} · \textbf{\hi{मे}} \emph{me} · \textbf{\hi{शि}} \emph{śi}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\textbf{\hi{शि}} — \emph{śi} or \emph{iś}? (\emph{\textbf{Śi}}.) Where is \hi{ि} written, and where is it pronounced? (\textbf{Before} the consonant on the page, \textbf{after} it in speech.) Does it add to the inherent vowel? (\textbf{No} — it replaces it.) Next: \hi{र} and \hi{स}, then your own name phrase.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ra, sa]{\hi{र} and \hi{स} — a spineless letter and a possible cousin}

\label{lesson:HI-W04-ra-sa-mera-naam}



\begin{quote}
Two more letters put every consonant in \textquotedblleft{}my name\textquotedblright{} within reach.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \hi{र} — \textquotedblleft{}ra\textquotedblright{}, your first spineless letter}
Every letter you have \emph{written} so far has had a \textbf{vertical spine on the right}. \hi{र} doesn't:

1. \textbf{a shoulder} — a small hook at the top left. 2. \textbf{a downstroke} — falling away from it. 3. \textbf{the top bar} — last.

That's all. A shoulder and a stroke.

\hi{र} is the first of these you write, but not the only one in the script — \textbf{\hi{द}} is spineless too, and you have already \emph{read} it in \emph{dhanyavād} (Chapter 1). Think of \textquotedblleft{}no right-hand post\textquotedblright{} as a small family to learn, not as \hi{र}'s private signature.

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \hi{स} — \textquotedblleft{}sa\textquotedblright{}}
Back to the normal frame, with a curl and a body:

1. \textbf{a left curl} 2. \textbf{a body} 3. \textbf{the right spine} 4. \textbf{the top bar} — last.

\#\#\# A possible very distant cousin

\textbf{\hi{स}} and English \textbf{S} may be related — and the story is worth telling carefully, because half of it is certain and half is not.

The certain half: English \textbf{S} comes from Latin, Latin from Greek \textbf{sigma}, and Greek from the \textbf{Phoenician} letter \emph{šin}. That western line is not in doubt.

The uncertain half: \textbf{Brahmi}, the ancestor of Devanagari, is \emph{most likely} descended from the same Semitic family, arriving in India by way of \textbf{Aramaic}. That is the leading scholarly view, but it is not settled — some scholars argue Brahmi was an indigenous invention, and even among those who accept a Semitic source, which letter became which is disputed.

So: if the mainstream account holds, \hi{स} and S share a great-great-grandparent some three thousand years back, with no family resemblance left at all. Say \textquotedblleft{}probably cousins,\textquotedblright{} not \textquotedblleft{}cousins.\textquotedblright{}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \hi{र} — \textquotedblleft{}shoulder, downstroke, bar\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{no spine}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \hi{स} — \textquotedblleft{}curl, body, spine, bar\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the probable cousins — \textquotedblleft{}sigma · S from \emph{šin} … and \textbf{probably} \hi{स} too\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What makes \textbf{\hi{र}} unlike the letters you've written so far? (\textbf{No right-hand spine} — just a shoulder and a downstroke.) Is it the only spineless letter? (\textbf{No} — \textbf{\hi{द}} is one too, and there are a few others.) Draw \textbf{\hi{स}} — four pieces? (Curl, body, spine, bar.) Which English letter might \hi{स} be related to, and how sure are we? (\textbf{S} — certainly \emph{šin} $\to$ sigma $\to$ S going west; the eastern leg through Aramaic to \textbf{Brahmi} is the \textbf{leading view, not settled}.) Next: assemble those letters into \textquotedblleft{}my name\textquotedblright{} and let the word boundary break the head-line.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[merā nām]{\hi{मेरा} \hi{नाम} — two words, two head-lines}

\label{lesson:HI-W04-write-mera-naam}



\begin{quote}
You now know every piece of \emph{merā nām}, \textquotedblleft{}my name.\textquotedblright{} This lesson only asks you to assemble them and make the word boundary visible.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — Build the phrase}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\hi{मेरा}} & \hi{म} + \hi{े} + \hi{र} + \hi{ा} — \emph{merā}, \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{} \\
\textbf{\hi{नाम}} & \hi{न} + \hi{ा} + \hi{म} — \emph{nām}, \textquotedblleft{}name\textquotedblright{} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{मेरा} \hi{नाम}}
\end{quote}

Two words means \textbf{two bars}. Modern Hindi separates words with an ordinary space, exactly like English. Because the shirorekhā is drawn over each word, that space appears as a \textbf{break in the line}. The gap in the bar is the result of the space, not a substitute for it.

Classical Sanskrit manuscripts often ran words together without spaces, so the bar could continue across a whole line. Modern Hindi does not ask you to copy that manuscript habit.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Write these out:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{मेरा}} — four pieces, one bar
  \item \textbf{\hi{नाम}} — three pieces, one bar
  \item \textbf{\hi{मेरा} \hi{नाम}} — two words, \textbf{two separate bars}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Write \textbf{\hi{मेरा} \hi{नाम}}. How many bars, and why? (\textbf{Two} — Hindi uses an ordinary \textbf{space}, and the bar breaks because of it.) Is the gap itself the space? (\textbf{No} — it is the visible result of the space.) Next: stop an inherent vowel, then use that power inside \emph{namaste}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(vowel killer)]{The vowel killer — virama and halant}

\label{lesson:HI-W05-virama-namaste}



\begin{quote}
Every consonant carries a free \textquotedblleft{}a.\textquotedblright{} Mātrās replace it. But what if you need \textbf{no vowel at all} — just a bare consonant?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The virama \hi{्}}
\textbf{\hi{्}} is the \textbf{virama} — a small stroke \textbf{below} the consonant that removes the inherent vowel:

\begin{quote}
\hi{क} = \emph{ka} $\to$ \hi{क्} = \emph{\textbf{k}}
\end{quote}

The name says exactly what it does. \textbf{\hi{विराम}} (\emph{virāma}) is \textquotedblleft{}a \textbf{stopping}, a cessation\textquotedblright{} — \emph{vi-} + \emph{ram-}, \textquotedblleft{}to rest, to come to a halt.\textquotedblright{} The vowel is told to stop.

And the word is still working elsewhere in Hindi punctuation: a full stop is \textbf{\hi{पूर्ण} \hi{विराम}} (\textquotedblleft{}\emph{complete} stop\textquotedblright{}), a comma is \textbf{\hi{अल्प} \hi{विराम}} (\textquotedblleft{}\emph{slight} stop\textquotedblright{}), a semicolon \textbf{\hi{अर्ध} \hi{विराम}} (\textquotedblleft{}\emph{half} stop\textquotedblright{}). One word, graded by how long you rest.

A naming note: \emph{virāma} is the Sanskrit term, and the one Unicode uses. In everyday Hindi the mark is usually called the \textbf{\hi{हलंत}} (\emph{halant}). Same mark, two names — you'll meet both.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \hi{क्} — \textquotedblleft{}\hi{क} with the stroke below\textquotedblright{} — the vowel is dead
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}virāma — stopping; halant — the everyday Hindi name\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \hi{क} \emph{ka} $\to$ \hi{क्} \emph{k}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the virama \textbf{\hi{्}} do, and what does its name mean? (Kills the \textbf{inherent vowel}; \emph{virāma} = \textquotedblleft{}a \textbf{stopping}\textquotedblright{} — and a full stop in Hindi is \textbf{\hi{पूर्ण} \hi{विराम}}, a \textquotedblleft{}complete stop\textquotedblright{}.) What is the mark usually called in everyday Hindi? (The \textbf{halant}.) Next: watch a stopped consonant squeeze into the one that follows.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sta]{\hi{स्त} — two consonants squeezed together}

\label{lesson:HI-W05-conjuncts}



\begin{quote}
A visible virama can stop a vowel. In ordinary writing, the stopped consonant often goes one step further and fuses with the consonant after it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The usual squeeze}
The fused shape is a \textbf{conjunct}:

\begin{quote}
\hi{स्} + \hi{त} $\to$ \textbf{\hi{स्त}} (\emph{sta})
\end{quote}

Look at \hi{स}. It loses its right-hand spine, shrinks, and leans into \hi{त}. For \textbf{spine-bearing} letters this is the usual move: \textbf{the first consonant gives up its spine and hands the syllable to the second}.

\subsection*{You'll want to know — Spineless and irregular shapes}
\hi{र} has no spine to give up, so it behaves differently: as a hook above a later letter (\hi{र्} + \hi{क} $\to$ \textbf{\hi{र्क}}) or as a small stroke under an earlier one (\hi{क} + \hi{्र} $\to$ \textbf{\hi{क्र}}). Other spineless letters, \textbf{\hi{द}} among them, stack or take special shapes. A few common conjuncts — \textbf{\hi{क्ष}}, \textbf{\hi{त्र}}, \textbf{\hi{ज्ञ}} — are irregular and must be learned whole.

This is why Devanagari seems to have so many shapes: it is not only 40-odd letters, but also the ligatures they form when they collide. Do not memorise every conjunct as a separate character. Learn to recognise the \emph{squeeze}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \hi{स्} — \hi{स} with the vowel stopped
  \item \emph{Write it:} \hi{स्त} — watch \hi{स} \textbf{lose its spine} and lean into \hi{त}
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \hi{र्क} and \hi{क्र} — two special jobs for spineless \hi{र}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What usually happens instead of leaving a virama visible? (The first consonant \textbf{fuses} with the next into a \textbf{conjunct}.) In \textbf{\hi{स्त}}, what does \hi{स} give up? (\textbf{Its spine}.) Why does \hi{र} need different forms? (\textbf{It has no spine to give up.}) Next: use \textbf{\hi{स्त}} inside the first greeting you learned.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[namaste]{\hi{नमस्ते} — assemble the greeting at last}

\label{lesson:HI-W05-write-namaste}



\begin{quote}
You have learned every piece separately. Now the writing track pays off in the first word of this book.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — Assemble \hi{नमस्ते}}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{piece} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\hi{न}} & \emph{na} & Lesson 1 \\
\textbf{\hi{म}} & \emph{ma} & Lesson 1 \\
\textbf{\hi{स्}} & \emph{s} — \hi{स} with its vowel killed & last lesson \\
\textbf{\hi{ते}} & \emph{te} — \hi{त} + the \hi{े} mātrā & Lessons 2 and 3 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{न} · \hi{म} · \hi{स्} · \hi{ते} $\to$ \hi{नमस्ते}}
\end{quote}

Write it, then draw \textbf{one bar} across the whole word.

\subsection*{You'll want to know — What you have been writing all along}
\textbf{\hi{नमस्ते}} joins \textbf{namas} + \textbf{te}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{namas} — \textquotedblleft{}a bow, an obeisance,\textquotedblright{} from \emph{nam-}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to bend}\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{te} — \textquotedblleft{}to you\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

So \emph{namaste} is literally \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}a bowing to you.\textquotedblright{}} It describes the physical gesture, which is why the word and folded hands go together. The greeting is the bow said aloud.

\emph{Namaskār} is the same \emph{namas} with \emph{kāra}, \textquotedblleft{}making\textquotedblright{}: \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{making} a bow.\textquotedblright{} One root, two greetings.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \hi{स्त} — the conjunct at the center
  \item \emph{Write it:} \hi{ते} — \hi{त} plus the stroke above
  \item \emph{Write it:} \textbf{\hi{नमस्ते}} — one bar across all of it
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}\emph{namas} = a \textbf{bow}, \emph{te} = \textbf{to you}\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Write \textbf{\hi{नमस्ते}}. How many bars? (\textbf{One} — it is one word.) What does it literally mean? (\textbf{A bowing to you}: \emph{namas}, \textquotedblleft{}bow,\textquotedblright{} + \emph{te}, \textquotedblleft{}to you.\textquotedblright{}) And \emph{namaskār}? (The same \emph{namas} + \emph{kāra}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{making} a bow.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 2 — the introduction, whole}

\label{lesson:HI-C02-practice}



\begin{quote}
Every atom is built and rooted. Here's the exchange it was for.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Hindi} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\hi{मेरा} \hi{नाम} \hi{मीरा} \hi{है।} (\emph{merā nām Mira hai}) & My name is Mira. \\
\hi{आपका} \hi{नाम} \hi{क्या} \hi{है}? (\emph{āpkā nām kyā hai}) & What's your name? \\
\hi{मेरा} \hi{नाम} \hi{अरुण} \hi{है।} (\emph{merā nām Arun hai}) & My name is Arun. \\
\hi{आपसे} \hi{मिलकर} \hi{ख़ुशी} \hi{हुई।} (\emph{āpse milkar khushī huī}) & Pleased to meet you. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Every atom traced:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{nām} $\leftarrow$ Sanskrit \emph{nāman} (English \textbf{name}, \textbf{noun})
  \item \textbf{merā} $\leftarrow$ root \emph{ma-} (English \textbf{me}, \textbf{my}, \textbf{mine})
  \item \textbf{hai} $\leftarrow$ Sanskrit \emph{asti} (English \textbf{is}, German \emph{ist}, Latin \emph{est})
  \item \textbf{kyā} $\leftarrow$ stem \emph{ka-} (English \textbf{what}, \textbf{who})
  \item \textbf{khushī} $\leftarrow$ Persian \emph{khush} (Hindi's second, Perso-Arabic vocabulary)
\end{itemize}

Two Hindi habits: the \textbf{verb goes last} (subject–object–verb), and \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} has \textbf{three} respect-levels (\emph{āp / tum / tū}).

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the whole exchange, both voices
  \item your own introduction — \textquotedblleft{}merā nām … hai\textquotedblright{}
  \item ask it back — \textquotedblleft{}āpkā nām kyā hai?\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give your name, ask someone else's, say you're pleased to meet them. (\emph{Merā nām … hai. / Āpkā nām kyā hai? / …khushī huī.}) Which two words here come from Hindi's Persian vocabulary rather than Sanskrit? (\emph{khushī} — and you'll recall \emph{shukriyā}, \emph{alvidā} from Ch1.)

Next chapter: \emph{āp kaise haiṁ?} (\textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{}) and answering with \emph{ṭhīk} — the responding cycle.
\end{tcolorbox}
